metadata.title: The Key and the Door — Extending walker-jumpman
metadata.note: Walker-mode godot-waikthrough. Gameplay beats B02-B08 are REAL engine capture at native 3840x2160, scripted input, labeled on screen; holds are labeled HELD FRAME. Two human playtests are recorded in the game's TEST-REPORT.md section 7. B00's prompt is an illustrative reconstruction, labeled as such. No upload.

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 1 — ClaudeComposerAsk. Prompt is an ILLUSTRATIVE RECONSTRUCTION, labeled on screen.
beats.narration_text: Annyeong — this is Liam, in for Bear. Bao Xing took Nik Bear Brown's walker-jumpman, a small Godot platformer with two gaps and a spike, and was asked to give it a new character and a new section. Here is the kind of ask that starts that work. This prompt is a reconstruction for the film, not a recording of the original session.

props.segment: The Key and the Door — illustrative reconstruction
props.command: Please use Walker to convert my game design document about a small, readable 2D platformer — one fixed-height jump, forgiving input windows, unlimited retries — into a playable Godot project. Then extend it: a new main character, and a new section built around a locked door and the key that opens it.
props.runningText: reconstructing the ask — not a transcript of the original session…
output: Starter: two gaps, a spike, a flag.
Added: a courier, a key, a door.

beats.role_note: WALKER BOOKEND 2 — what was ACTUALLY built. Hesitant-writer correction.
beats.narration_text: What exists is not a new game. It is the starter, unmodified below x nine hundred and sixty, plus two additions: a character called the Lamp-Head Courier, and a locked door with the key that opens it. Fifty-three automated checks pass, twenty-five of them the starter's own, unaltered. Cherries, audio, settings and an export are still not built, and this film will not pretend otherwise.

beats.role_note: CAUSE AND EFFECT 1 — the required source-change-to-behaviour link. Two numbers from the starter's tuning decide the whole trap.
beats.narration_text: That trap is not a timer and not a random event. It is two numbers from the starter's tuning, untouched. Standing, the player's collider occupies y two ninety-two to three twenty. At the top of a jump it occupies two thirty-six to two sixty-four. Those two bands do not overlap. So an arming rectangle placed between them, at two forty-four to two eighty-four, is provably unreachable on foot and provably reachable in the air. Walking can never spring it. Leaving the ground always will.

show.event: arming rectangle 244-284 drops into the gap
WALK = never arms / JUMP = always arms

props.title: Two bands that never meet.
props.sparkLine: The trap is geometry, not timing.
details:
walk = never arms
jump = always arms

beats.role_note: CAUSE AND EFFECT 2 — the probe. Same arithmetic that killed the first layout now proves the barrier works.
beats.narration_text: The same arithmetic shaped the rest. A reachability probe sweeps real takeoff positions through real physics, and it is how every landing here was chosen: seventy pixels onto the first ledge, fifty-six and fifty-eight between them, thirty-eight across the gap, ten to bait the trap. Look at the fourth line. Ledge D to the merge platform: unreachable. That is not a defect — that is the barrier doing its job, measured rather than assumed.

props.title: Every landing chosen by measurement.
props.sparkLine: Change the geometry, not the jump.
lines: floor -> B  (+48 rise)      takeoff window 70 px
L1 -> M     (56px gap)      takeoff window 38 px
walk-under B and C          clear, 0 jumps

beats.role_note: VERDICT LAW — observed / by-design / untested / next. Must not overclaim, and must name what the key cost the design.
beats.narration_text: Verdict. Observed working: the trap punishes the jump and spares the walk; the key cannot be taken on foot; the door will not open without it; and fifty-three checks pass with the starter's twenty-five unaltered. Two humans finished it, and the second had never seen the design — he met the trap cold, died to it, and worked out the bait unaided. By design, and this is the honest part: making the key mandatory cost this level its fork. It used to ask the player to choose a line. Now it asks them to notice a locked door and go and find what opens it. That is sequencing, not a decision, and it is the weaker prompt. Next improvement: log where deaths actually happen, so the next playtest returns numbers instead of impressions.

props.artifactHeading: The Key and the Door — extending walker-jumpman.
artifactLines: Observed: trap punishes the jump, spares the walk; key needs a jump.
Observed: the door will not open without the key. 53 checks pass.
Tested cold: a second player died to the trap, then solved it unaided.
By design: a mandatory key cost this level its fork — sequencing, not choice.
Next: log where deaths happen, so a playtest yields numbers.

beats.role_note: YOUR TURN LAW — a runnable prompt relevant to THIS video, read in full. Liam signs off here.
beats.narration_text: Your turn. If you are extending someone else's level, paste this before you commit to a layout: 'Read this project's tuning values, then write a throwaway script that sweeps real takeoff positions through the real physics and tells me which of my planned jumps actually land. Do not change the jump to make my layout work.' Bao's probe rejected a design he had already hand-computed and believed. The moment you reach for jump strength, you have stopped extending the game and started editing it to agree with you. Liam, in for Bear.
